cor-ss-ms-distributions.title: Distributions of the mean squares
cor-ss-ms-distributions.html: Let Y∼Nn(μ,σ2I) with μ∈C(X), and let V1,…,Vk be an analysis of variance decomposition of C(X). Then the sums of squares Y⊤P1Y,…,Y⊤PkY and SSE are mutually independent, Y⊤PiYσ2∼χ2(ri, γi),γi=‖Piμ‖2σ2,SSEσ2∼χ2(n−r), and Fi=MSi/s2∼F(ri,n−r,γi), which is central iff Piμ=0. The same holds for a single projection P onto any subspace of C(X), such as a partial sum of squares, paired with SSE.

cor-ss-orthogonal-coefficients.title: Coefficients in orthogonal designs
cor-ss-orthogonal-coefficients.html: Suppose X=[1,X1,…,Xk] has full column rank and satisfies the conditions of @thm-ss-orthogonal-design. Then the least squares coefficients of the columns of Xj are the same in every model that contains 1 and Xj, whichever other terms it contains. Only the intercept changes.

cor-ss-single-column.title: The extra sum of squares of one column
cor-ss-single-column.title_html: The extra sum of squares of one column
cor-ss-single-column.html: Let X have full column rank p, write cjj for the jth diagonal entry of (X⊤X)−1, and let X(j) be X without its jth column. Then SS(xj∣X(j))=β^j2cjj=tj2s2,tj=β^jscjj,s2=SSEn−p. Consequently, the ratio of this one-degree-of-freedom sum of squares to the residual mean square is tj2.

def-ss-anova-decomposition.title: Analysis of variance decomposition
def-ss-anova-decomposition.html: An analysis of variance decomposition of the model space is a list of subspaces V1,…,Vk of C(X) that are mutually orthogonal and whose sum is C(X): C(X)=V1⊕V2⊕⋯⊕Vk,Vi⊥Vj (i≠j). The subspace Vk+1=C(X)⊥ is the error space. Writing Pi for the orthogonal projection onto Vi, the sum of squares for Vi is ‖Piy‖2=y⊤Piy, its degrees of freedom are ri=dim⁡Vi, and its mean square is ‖Piy‖2/ri.

def-ss-extra.title: Extra sum of squares
def-ss-extra.html: Let X1 and X2 be matrices with n rows, let X=[X1,X2], and let M1 and M be the projections onto C(X1) and C(X). The extra sum of squares of X2 given X1 is SS(X2∣X1)=y⊤(M−M1)y=SSE(X1)−SSE(X), with rank(X)−rank(X1) degrees of freedom. Here SSE(⋅) is the residual sum of squares of the model with the given model matrix.

def-ss-partial.title: Partial sums of squares; Types II and III
def-ss-partial.title_html: Partial sums of squares; Types II and III
def-ss-partial.html:
For a model with terms X0,X1,…,Xk, write X(−j) for X with the columns of Xj removed.

  1. The partial (or last-in) sum of squares of Xj is SS(Xj∣X(−j))=y⊤(M−M(−j))y, where M(−j) projects onto C(X(−j)).

  2. The Type II sum of squares of Xj is its extra sum of squares given all terms that do not contain it: SS(Xj∣Xi: Xi does not contain Xj, i≠j).

  3. The Type III sum of squares of Xj is its partial sum of squares (a) computed when every factor is coded by sum-to-zero contrast columns and every interaction by the products of the columns of its factors.

def-ss-partial-r2.title: Partial coefficient of determination
def-ss-partial-r2.html: Let C(X1)⊆C(X) with 1∈C(X1). The partial coefficient of determination of X over X1 is RX∣X12=SSE(X1)−SSE(X)SSE(X1)=SS(X∣X1)SSE(X1), the proportion of the residual variation of the reduced model that the larger model explains.

def-ss-sequential.title: Sequential sums of squares
def-ss-sequential.html: The sequential (or Type I) sum of squares of the term Xj, for the order X0,X1,…,Xk, is SS(Xj∣X0,…,Xj−1)=y⊤(Mj−Mj−1)y,j=1,…,k, with dj=rank(Mj)−rank(Mj−1) degrees of freedom.

eq-ss-adjusted-r2.html: R¯2=1−s2sy2=1−(1−R2)n−1n−r.

eq-ss-anova-identity.html: ‖y‖2=‖P1y‖2+⋯+‖Pky‖2+‖(I−M)y‖2;

eq-ss-ems.html: E(MSi)=σ2+‖Piμ‖2ri.

eq-ss-f-mean.html: E(Fi)=n−rn−r−2⋅ri+γiri.

eq-ss-hypothesis.html: SSH=(Λ⊤β^−d)⊤(Λ⊤GΛ)−1(Λ⊤β^−d).

eq-ss-proportional.html: nij=ni⋅n⋅jnfor all i,j.

exm-ss-adding-crime.title: Adding poverty and urbanization
exm-ss-adding-crime.html: In the state data, fit the murder rate on single parenthood first: y^=−8.2146+0.5147xsingle, with residual sum of squares 121.92. Now add Z=[xpoverty,xurban]. The listing computes γ^=(0.2538,0.0046) from the old residual projection alone, and corrects the old coefficients to −9.0946 and 0.3980. These agree with a fresh fit of the enlarged model. The residual sum of squares falls by 19.96, on 2 degrees of freedom, to 101.96. Single parenthood’s coefficient drops by almost a quarter once poverty is allowed to take its share, the pattern seen in @exm-proj-sequential-order.

exm-ss-anes-types.title: Party, education and political self-placement
exm-ss-anes-types.html:
In the 1996 American National Election Study, 944 respondents placed themselves on a seven-point scale from extremely liberal (1) to extremely conservative (7). Classify them by party identification (Democrat, Independent, Republican, counting those who only lean to a party as Independents) and by education (high school or less, college, graduate study). The cell counts and means are:

high school college graduate
Democrat 146, 3.97 108, 3.43 126, 2.92
Independent 80, 4.39 64, 4.28 95, 4.09
Republican 87, 5.40 105, 5.36 133, 5.40

The design is unbalanced, and education is associated with party: 38% of the Democrats but only 27% of the Republicans have at most a high school education. The pattern of means shows an interaction. Among Democrats self-placement moves left with education by more than a scale point, while among Republicans it does not move at all. The sums of squares for the terms are:

Term df Type I, party first Type I, education first Type II Type III reference coding
party 2 647.46 674.42 674.42 650.41 112.27
education 2 43.26 16.31 43.26 32.03 75.12
interaction 4 35.81 35.81 35.81 35.81 35.81
residual 935 1224.62 1224.62 1224.62 1224.62 1224.62

The two Type I columns each add up to the model sum of squares 726.54, up to rounding. The other columns do not: the Type II entries add up to more. Education receives 16.31 when entered first and 43.26 after party. Since the least educated group contains the most Democrats, who are the most liberal, the marginal comparison mixes the leftward drift of educated Democrats with the partisan composition of each education group, and the two partly cancel. The Type III sum of squares 32.03 tests whether the unweighted averages over the three parties of the education means are equal. The last column, computed with reference coding, answers different questions: 75.12 for education measures the education gradient among Democrats only (the first party level), which is the steepest, and 112.27 for party compares the parties among respondents with a high school education only. The interaction row is the same in every column because the interaction is the highest-order term.

exm-ss-crime-adjusted.title: Adjusted R^2 for the state data
exm-ss-crime-adjusted.title_html: Adjusted R2 for the state data
exm-ss-crime-adjusted.html:
For all seven models built from poverty, single parenthood and urbanization (each with an intercept):

Regressors R2 R¯2
poverty 0.3599 0.3466
single 0.5719 0.5629
urban 0.0221 0.0017
poverty, single 0.6410 0.6257
poverty, urban 0.4626 0.4398
single, urban 0.5844 0.5668
all three 0.6419 0.6186

R2 is largest for the full model, as it must be. R¯2 prefers poverty and single parenthood without urbanization. Adding urbanization to that model raises R2 slightly but lowers R¯2, because its t statistic in the full model is only 0.349, so its F ratio is 0.121<1.

exm-ss-crime-anova.title: An analysis of variance table for murder rates
exm-ss-crime-anova.title_html: An analysis of variance table for murder rates
exm-ss-crime-anova.html:
Return to the regression of the 2009 murder rate of the 50 US states on poverty, single parenthood and urbanization, with an intercept (@exm-proj-fwl-crime). Here r=4 and y¯=4.514. The listing computes every sum of squares from the coordinates of y in an orthonormal basis of C(X), as in @thm-ss-decomposition(d): the first coordinate gives the mean, the next three the regression.

Source df Sum of squares Mean square
Mean 1 1018.81 1018.81
Regression 3 182.80 60.93
Residual 46 101.96 2.217
Total (uncorrected) 50 1303.57
Total (corrected) 49 284.76

The regression mean square is 27.49 times the residual mean square. If none of the three regressors were related to the murder rate and the errors were normal, a ratio this large would occur with probability about 2.5×10−10. The proportion of the corrected total that the regression accounts for is 182.80/284.76=0.6419, the R2 of @thm-proj-r2-cosine.

exm-ss-crime-partial.title: Partial R^2 in the state data
exm-ss-crime-partial.title_html: Partial R2 in the state data
exm-ss-crime-partial.html:
In the three-regressor model, with n−r=46:

Regressor t partial R2 R2 without it
poverty 2.718 0.1383 0.5844
single 4.799 0.3337 0.4626
urban 0.349 0.0026 0.6410

Each partial R2 equals t2/(t2+46), and each row satisfies part (a): for poverty, 1−0.6419=(1−0.5844)(1−0.1383). Poverty explains 14% of the variation that single parenthood and urbanization leave unexplained, although on its own it explains 36% of the total (R2=0.3599). For the pair poverty and urbanization over single parenthood, the F ratio on 2 and 46 degrees of freedom is 4.502 and the partial R2 is 0.1637.

exm-ss-education-contrasts.title: Splitting the education sum of squares
exm-ss-education-contrasts.title_html: Splitting the education sum of squares
exm-ss-education-contrasts.html: Consider the 944 self-placements of @exm-ss-anes-types by education alone. The group sizes are 313, 277 and 354, and the group means are 4.476, 4.357 and 4.167. The between-groups sum of squares is 16.306 on two degrees of freedom. The contrast of college against graduate, c2=(0,1,−1), has sum of squares 5.653. The contrast of high school against the other two, weighted by their sizes, c1=(1,−0.439,−0.561), is orthogonal to c2 in the sense above, and has sum of squares 10.652. The two add up to the between-groups sum of squares, up to rounding. The more obvious contrast (1,−12,−12), high school against the plain average of the others, has sum of squares 9.534, and together with c2 it gives 15.187: with unequal group sizes it is not orthogonal to c2.

exm-ss-ems-simulation.title: Checking expected mean squares by simulation
exm-ss-ems-simulation.title_html: Checking expected mean squares by simulation
exm-ss-ems-simulation.html:
Take the design of @exm-ss-anes-types: n=944 respondents in the nine cells of party by education, with the observed counts. Set the true cell means equal to the observed cell means, and σ2=1.21. The script generates 40,000 data sets with normal errors and 40,000 with centred exponential errors of the same variance, which are strongly skewed. For each it computes the sequential decomposition (party, then education, then interaction), the residual, and the Type III sum of squares for party, and averages the mean squares:

Source df γ E(MS) normal skewed Var(MS) simulated
mean 1 14594.91 17661.050 17660.423 17661.259 85476.55 86357.17
party 2 535.09 324.942 324.915 324.787 784.89 786.39
education given party 2 35.75 22.840 22.836 22.891 53.81 53.13
interaction 4 29.60 10.163 10.174 10.179 11.57 11.75
residual 935 0.00 1.210 1.210 1.210 0.0031 0.0031
party, Type III 2 537.53 326.414 326.362 326.259 788.46 789.47

The columns E(MS) and Var(MS) come from @eq-ss-ems and @thm-ss-expected-mean-squares(d), with Var(MSi)=σ4(2ri+4γi)/ri2; the last column is the simulated variance under normal errors. The averages agree with the expectations under both error distributions, as parts (a) and (b) promise. The variances are another matter. Under skewed errors the variance of the residual mean square is 0.0124, 3.97 times the normal-theory value, because the variance of a quadratic form involves the fourth moment of the errors (@thm-rv-quadform-variance). And the correlation between the interaction and residual mean squares, 0.008 under normal errors (zero in theory), is 0.020 under skewed errors, against a theoretical 0.025 from the third and fourth moments: the two mean squares are no longer independent.

For the interaction, the noncentrality γ=29.60 is large. By @eq-ss-f-mean, the F ratio has mean 8.417, and the simulated mean is 8.427. Its 5% critical value is 2.381, and the power is 0.9967 in theory and 0.9967 in the simulation. Figure 9.6.1 shows the simulated distribution with the noncentral F density.

exm-ss-grunfeld-balanced.title: Firms and years
exm-ss-grunfeld-balanced.html:
Grunfeld’s investment panel (@exm-proj-grunfeld) records 11 firms in each of 20 years, one observation per firm and year. As a two-way layout with factors firm and year, it has nij=1, so @eq-ss-proportional holds, and the additive model’s sums of squares for the logarithm of investment are order-free:

Source df Sum of squares
firm 10 473.482
year 19 26.749
residual 190 14.667
corrected total 219 514.898

Firms differ enormously in the scale of their investment, and years matter much less. Adding the logarithm of market value as a covariate destroys the orthogonality, because value varies with both firm and year. The sum of squares for firm then depends on what else is in the model: it is 90.701 after year and value, and 88.443 after value alone. Most of the variation between firms is variation in size, which value already measures. This is the setting of analysis of covariance (Chapter 18).

exm-ss-hypothesis-crime.title: Equal effects of poverty and single parenthood
exm-ss-hypothesis-crime.title_html: Equal effects of poverty and single parenthood
exm-ss-hypothesis-crime.html: Both poverty and single parenthood are percentages of the population. Is one percentage point of either associated with the same change in the murder rate? The hypothesis is λ⊤β=0 with λ=(0,1,−1,0)⊤. Formula @eq-ss-hypothesis gives SSH=1.807 on one degree of freedom, identical to the drop in residual sum of squares when the two regressors are replaced by their sum. Its ratio to the residual mean square is 0.815, so the data are entirely compatible with equal effects. For a hypothesis with a nonzero right-hand side, βsingle=0.5, @thm-ss-restricted gives the constrained coefficients 0.1803 for poverty and −0.0044 for urbanization, and a sum of squares of 3.357, both confirmed by a direct fit of the reduced model.

exm-ss-nile-polynomials.title: A trend in the Nile
exm-ss-nile-polynomials.html:
The annual flow of the Nile at Aswan was recorded for the 100 years 1871–1970. How much of its variation is a smooth trend? The listing builds the orthonormal polynomials q0,…,q4 for the years by a QR factorization of the matrix of powers, and reads off the sequential sums of squares (in units of (108m3)2):

Degree 1 2 3 4
Sequential sum of squares 613893 309415 1894 134142

The corrected total is 2835157. The linear term accounts for a fraction 0.217 of it, and the first three terms together for 0.326. Against the residual mean square of the cubic fit, 19895 on 96 degrees of freedom, the quadratic component has F=15.55 and the cubic only 0.10. The quartic sum of squares is large again, a sign that the pattern is not a gentle polynomial at all. The flow dropped abruptly around the end of the nineteenth century (Cobb 1978), and a low-degree polynomial can only approximate a step (Figure 9.4.1).

With the raw powers of the centred and scaled year, the sums of squares depend on the order: the linear column entered after the quadratic and cubic ones receives 74751 instead of 613893. The raw linear coefficient is −134.4 in the linear and quadratic fits, but −117.3 in the cubic and quartic ones. It survives the quadratic term because the years are symmetric about their mean, which makes odd and even centred powers orthogonal (@exr-ss-symmetric-design), but not the cubic term. The coefficient of q1 is −783.5 in every fit.

exm-ss-no-intercept.title: Forcing the murder regression through the origin
exm-ss-no-intercept.title_html: Forcing the murder regression through the origin
exm-ss-no-intercept.html: Refit the model of @exm-ss-crime-anova without the intercept. The residual sum of squares rises from 101.96 to 177.73, so the fit is much worse. Yet the residuals now sum to −8.332, and the would-be corrected identity is off by −2y¯∑iε^i=75.22: the corrected total 284.76 is not 31.81+177.73=209.54. The uncentred ratio ‖Y^‖2/‖y‖2, which some software reports as R2 for such models, is 0.8637, much larger than the 0.6419 of the better model with an intercept (@exr-proj-uncentred-r2).

exr-ss-averaging.title: B2
exr-ss-averaging.html: Suppose each of g distinct values x1,…,xg carries m observations. Show that the least squares line fitted to all gm observations is the same as the line fitted to the g group means, and that its R2 for the individual data is at most its R2 for the means, with equality iff every observation equals its group mean.

exr-ss-balanced-types.title: B1
exr-ss-balanced-types.html: In a two-way layout with interaction and nij=m≥1 for all cells, show that the Type I sums of squares of A in either order, and its Type II and Type III sums of squares, are all equal to bm∑i(y¯i⋅⋅−y¯⋅⋅⋅)2.

exr-ss-canonical-form.title: B1
exr-ss-canonical-form.html: Let U=[Q1,…,Qk+1] be the orthogonal matrix of @thm-ss-decomposition(d) and z=U⊤Y. Suppose E(Y)=μ∈C(X) and Cov(Y)=σ2I. Show that the coordinates of z are uncorrelated with variance σ2, that the last n−r of them have mean zero, and deduce E(SSE)=(n−r)σ2. Show that if in addition Y is normal, the coordinates are independent.

exr-ss-chain-product.title: B3
exr-ss-chain-product.html: Using part (d) of @thm-ss-partial-r2 and the sequential sums of squares of @exm-proj-sequential-order (order A), express 1−R2 for the three-regressor model as a product of three factors, and identify each factor as one minus a partial R2.

exr-ss-design-r2.title: B1
exr-ss-design-r2.html: In simple regression with fixed x values, E(Y)=β01+β1x and Cov(Y)=σ2I, use @thm-rv-quadform-mean to show that E(SSR)=σ2+β12Sxx and E(SST)=(n−1)σ2+β12Sxx. Show that the ratio of these expectations tends to 1 as Sxx→∞ with n fixed, and to 1/(n−1) as Sxx→0, and interpret the second limit.

exr-ss-empty-cell.title: B4
exr-ss-empty-cell.html: Suppose that in a 2×2 layout the cell (2,2) is empty. Show that μ¯1⋅−μ¯2⋅ is not estimable. Compute what the last-in sum of squares of A under sum-to-zero coding tests in this case. Hint: with a cell missing, the interaction columns restricted to the observed cells are no longer independent of the main-effect columns.

exr-ss-extra-max.title: C1
exr-ss-extra-max.html: Using @exr-ss-max-single and @lem-ss-residualized, show that SS(X2∣X1)=maxa(a⊤X~2⊤y)2a⊤X~2⊤X~2a, the maximum being over a with X~2a≠0. Deduce that the extra sum of squares of a block is at least that of any single column of the block, given X1, and that the sum of squares of an estimable hypothesis Λ⊤β=0 equals maxa(a⊤Λ⊤β^)2/(a⊤Λ⊤GΛa).

exr-ss-fill-table.title: A2
exr-ss-fill-table.html: A regression with an intercept has a corrected table in which the regression row has 3 degrees of freedom and sum of squares 120, the residual mean square is 2.5, and the corrected total sum of squares is 172.5. Find n, the residual degrees of freedom, the F ratio and R2.

exr-ss-four-point.title: A1
exr-ss-four-point.html: With x=1,2,3,4 and y=(3,5,4,8)⊤, use the orthogonal polynomial contrasts for four equally spaced points to compute the linear, quadratic and cubic sums of squares, and check that they add up to the corrected total sum of squares.

exr-ss-hypothesis-noncentrality.title: B3
exr-ss-hypothesis-noncentrality.html: In the setting of @thm-ss-hypothesis with d=0, show that the expected sum of squares of the hypothesis Λ⊤β=0 is σ2q+(Λ⊤β)⊤(Λ⊤GΛ)−1Λ⊤β, so the noncentrality is obtained by evaluating @eq-ss-hypothesis at the true parameter.

exr-ss-kurtosis-sse.title: C1
exr-ss-kurtosis-sse.html: Let the errors be independent with mean zero, variance σ2 and fourth moment μ4=E(εi4), and let μ∈C(X). Use @thm-rv-quadform-variance to show that Var(SSE)=(μ4−3σ4)∑i(1−hii)2+2σ4(n−r), where hii are the leverages. For the centred exponential errors of @exm-ss-ems-simulation, μ4=9σ4. Show that Var(s2)≈8σ4/(n−r) when all leverages are small, and compare with the simulated variance of the residual mean square.

exr-ss-list-types.title: A1
exr-ss-list-types.html: For a two-way model with terms A, B and AB, write each of the Type I sums of squares (both orders), the Type II sums of squares and the partial sums of squares in the notation SS(⋅∣⋅). Which of them are equal for every data set, whatever the design?

exr-ss-max-single.title: C1
exr-ss-max-single.html: Let V be a subspace with projection P. Show that ‖Py‖2=maxv∈V, v≠0(v⊤y)2v⊤v, with the maximum attained at v=Py when Py≠0. Interpret: the sum of squares of a row with ri degrees of freedom is the largest one-degree-of-freedom sum of squares obtainable by refining that row. Chapter 13 uses this fact to build Scheffé’s simultaneous intervals.

exr-ss-negative-r2.title: B2
exr-ss-negative-r2.html: For a model without an intercept, the quantity 1−SSE/SST is sometimes reported as R2. Show that it is negative iff the model fits worse than the intercept-only model. Construct a data set with n=4 and one regressor for which it is below −1.

exr-ss-no-variance-change.title: C2
exr-ss-no-variance-change.html: @exr-mat-adding-regressors gives the matrix inequality behind the remark after @thm-ss-adding. Using part (d) of that theorem instead, show that Var(β^W,j)=Var(β^j) iff the jth row of L is zero, and that this holds for every j iff X⊤Z=0. Show that when X⊤Z=0 the estimates β^ do not change at all.

exr-ss-not-monotone.title: B1
exr-ss-not-monotone.html: Prove the chain rule SS(X2,X3∣X1)=SS(X2∣X1)+SS(X3∣X1,X2), and deduce SS(X3∣X1,X2)≤SS(X2,X3∣X1). Show by an example from @exm-ss-adding-crime or its listing that SS(X3∣X1,X2)≤SS(X3∣X1) can fail.

exr-ss-omitted-term.title: B2
exr-ss-omitted-term.html: Suppose E(Y)=Xβ+zδ but the model E(Y)=Xβ is fitted, with 1∈C(X). Show that E(SSE)=σ2(n−r)+δ2‖(I−M)z‖2,E(SSR)=σ2(r−1)+‖(M−P1)(Xβ+zδ)‖2. Give an example in which β has all slopes zero but the regression mean square is inflated.

exr-ss-one-way-helmert.title: B3
exr-ss-one-way-helmert.html: In a one-way layout with g groups of equal size m, show that the Helmert contrasts ck=(1,…,1,−(k−1),0,…,0), with k−1 leading ones, k=2,…,g, are mutually orthogonal, and write the between-groups sum of squares as a sum of g−1 single-degree-of-freedom sums of squares. What goes wrong with unequal group sizes?

exr-ss-oneway-contrast.title: B3
exr-ss-oneway-contrast.html: In the one-way layout with model matrix X=[1,z1,…,zg] and group sizes n1,…,ng, use the generalized inverse G=diag(0,1/n1,…,1/ng) in @eq-ss-hypothesis to show that the sum of squares for α1=α2 is (y¯1−y¯2)2/(1/n1+1/n2). Verify with @prp-ss-effective-df that the constraint α1=0 has zero degrees of freedom.

exr-ss-oneway-ems.title: A2
exr-ss-oneway-ems.html: In a one-way layout with g groups, group sizes ni and means μi, show that the between-groups mean square has expectation σ2+∑ini(μi−μ¯)2/(g−1), where μ¯=∑iniμi/n. Compare with @exm-qf-oneway-cochran.

exr-ss-partial-sum-sign.title: C1
exr-ss-partial-sum-sign.html: With the notation of @exr-ss-two-regressor-formula, show that SS(x1∣1,x2)+SS(x2∣1,x1)−SSRSST=r12[r12(ry12+ry22)−2ry1ry2]1−r122. Deduce that the partial sums of squares add up to the regression sum of squares when r12=0, that they add up to less when ry1=ry2≠0 and 0<r12<1, and give correlations for which they add up to more.

exr-ss-power-design.title: C2
exr-ss-power-design.html: For the Type I sum of squares of A entered first in a two-way layout, show that its noncentrality can be positive when μij=βj depends on B only, and find the condition on the counts nij under which it is zero for all such μ. Relate your answer to @thm-ss-proportional.

exr-ss-proportional-not-equal.title: B2
exr-ss-proportional-not-equal.html: Take counts n11=1, n12=2, n21=2, n22=4. Check @eq-ss-proportional. Find cell means for which the Type III hypothesis for A holds but the Type I (and Type II) hypothesis fails.

exr-ss-r2-f-numbers.title: A1
exr-ss-r2-f-numbers.html: A regression with an intercept, n=20 and r=6 has R2=0.40. Compute R¯2 and the overall F ratio. Is R¯2 positive? Is it consistent with part (b) of @prp-ss-adjusted-r2?

exr-ss-r2-monotone-power.title: C1
exr-ss-r2-monotone-power.html: Under the conditions of @thm-ss-r2-null, show that for every c∈(0,1) the probability Pr(R2>c) is a strictly increasing function of the noncentrality γ. Hint: part (a) of the theorem and @thm-qf-f-power.

exr-ss-random-oneway.title: B1
exr-ss-random-oneway.html: In a balanced one-way layout with g groups of m observations, let Yij=μ+ai+εij, where the ai and εij are uncorrelated random variables with mean zero and variances σa2 and σ2. Show that Cov(Y)=σ2I+σa2ZZ⊤, with Z the matrix of group indicators, and use @thm-rv-quadform-mean to show that E(MSbetween)=σ2+mσa2,E(MSwithin)=σ2. Which ratio tests σa2=0, and what unbiased estimator of σa2 do the two mean squares suggest?

exr-ss-restricted-moments.title: B2
exr-ss-restricted-moments.html: In @thm-ss-restricted with Cov(Y)=σ2I, show that Cov(β^H)=σ2[C−CΛ(Λ⊤CΛ)−1Λ⊤C], that Cov(β^)−Cov(β^H) is nonnegative definite, and that E(β^H)=β when the constraint is true. What is E(β^H) when it is false?

exr-ss-simple-anova.title: A1
exr-ss-simple-anova.html: For simple regression, X=[1,x] with x not constant, show that SSR=β^12Sxx=Sxy2/Sxx and that the F ratio of the corrected table equals t2, where t=β^1Sxx/s.

exr-ss-simple-ems.title: A1
exr-ss-simple-ems.html: In simple regression with E(Y)=β01+β1x, show that the regression mean square has expectation σ2+β12Sxx, and that the F ratio of the corrected table has noncentrality β12Sxx/σ2 under normality.

exr-ss-simple-hypothesis.title: A1
exr-ss-simple-hypothesis.html: In simple regression, compute SSH for β1=0 from @eq-ss-hypothesis and show that it equals β^12Sxx, in agreement with @exr-ss-simple-anova.

exr-ss-small-layouts.title: A2
exr-ss-small-layouts.html: Which of the 2×2 count tables (2436), (2442) and (1339) give orthogonal centred factor spaces? For the one that does not, compute the inner product of the two centred indicator vectors of the first levels.

exr-ss-suppression-r2.title: C2
exr-ss-suppression-r2.html: For two regressors with sample correlations ry1=0.5, ry2=0 and r12=0.6, compute R2 and compare it with ry12+ry22. Use the formulas of @exr-ss-two-regressor-formula. Explain geometrically why a regressor that is uncorrelated with the response can raise R2.

exr-ss-symmetric-design.title: C1
exr-ss-symmetric-design.html: Suppose the design points are symmetric about their mean: after sorting, xi−x¯=−(xn+1−i−x¯). Show that every odd power of the centred variable is orthogonal to every even power (including the zeroth), that qk is an even or odd vector according to the parity of k, and explain the pattern of raw coefficients in @exm-ss-nile-polynomials.

exr-ss-two-regressor-formula.title: B1
exr-ss-two-regressor-formula.html: Let X=[1,x1,x2], and let ry1, ry2 and r12 be the sample correlations among y, x1 and x2, with |r12|<1. Show that SS(x2∣1)SST=ry22,SS(x2∣1,x1)SST=(ry2−ry1r12)21−r122. Show that adjusting for x1 increases the sum of squares of x2 whenever ry2=0 and ry1r12≠0, and find the condition for it in general.

exr-ss-two-way-constraints.title: C3
exr-ss-two-way-constraints.html: In the additive two-way model E(Yijk)=μ+αi+βj with all cells occupied, use @prp-ss-effective-df to find the degrees of freedom of the extra sums of squares for the constraints (i) ∑iαi=0 and ∑jβj=0; (ii) α1=α2; (iii) α1=0 and α1=α2.

exr-ss-type1-leak.title: B3
exr-ss-type1-leak.html: Take a=b=2, counts n11=n22=9 and n12=n21=1, and additive cell means μij=βj with β1=0 and β2=1, so that A has no effect. Compute the weighted row means μ¯iw and show that the hypothesis addressed by the Type I sum of squares of A entered first is false. What do the Type II and Type III hypotheses say here?

exr-ss-uncorrelated-regressors.title: A3
exr-ss-uncorrelated-regressors.html: Show that if the regressors x1,…,xk of a model with an intercept are pairwise uncorrelated, then R2=∑jryj2, where ryj is the sample correlation of y and xj.

exr-ss-weights-coincide.title: B2
exr-ss-weights-coincide.html: Show that the hypotheses of @thm-ss-two-way-hypotheses(a) and (b) are the same subspace of cell means iff nij=ni⋅/b for all i,j, that is, iff within every row all cells have the same count. Show that under proportional frequencies, nij=ni⋅n⋅j/n (@thm-ss-proportional), the hypothesis (a) compares row means weighted by the column proportions n⋅j/n, the same weights in every row.

lem-ss-residualized.title: Extra sums of squares by residualizing
lem-ss-residualized.title_html: Extra sums of squares by residualizing
lem-ss-residualized.html: For any X1 and X2, let X~2=(I−M1)X2. Then C([X1,X2])=C(X1)⊕C(X~2) with the two summands orthogonal, so M=M1+PC(X~2) and SS(X2∣X1)=‖PC(X~2)y‖2=y⊤X~2(X~2⊤X~2)−X~2⊤y.

prp-ss-adjusted-r2.title: Properties of the adjusted R^2
prp-ss-adjusted-r2.title_html: Properties of the adjusted R2
prp-ss-adjusted-r2.html:
Let 1∈C(X), 1≤r=rank(X)<n, and let F be the overall F ratio of @thm-ss-r2-null.

  1. R¯2≤R2, with equality iff r=1 or R2=1.

  2. For r>1, R¯2<0 iff F<1.

  3. If a model with rank r0 is enlarged to one of rank r=r0+q containing it, then R¯2 increases iff the F ratio of the added terms, [SS(added∣old)/q]/s2, exceeds 1. For a single added column this means |t|>1.

  4. Among models for the same response, R¯2 is largest for the model with the smallest residual mean square s2.

  5. Under the normal model with μ∈span(1), E(R¯2)=0.

prp-ss-computing-formulas.title: Computing the sums of squares
prp-ss-computing-formulas.html:
Let β^ be any least squares estimate. Then:

  1. ‖My‖2=β^⊤X⊤y and SSE=y⊤y−β^⊤X⊤y;

  2. if 1∈C(X), then SSR=β^⊤X⊤y−ny¯2;

  3. if X=[1,X1] has full column rank and X~1=(I−P1)X1 is the matrix of centred regressors, then SSR=β^1⊤X~1⊤X~1β^1=β^1⊤X~1⊤y, where β^1 holds the slopes.

prp-ss-effective-df.title: How much a constraint restricts
prp-ss-effective-df.html: For any p×q matrix Λ, the subspace S0={Xb:Λ⊤b=0} has dimension r−dim⁡(C(Λ)∩C(X⊤)). So the extra sum of squares for the constraint has dim⁡(C(Λ)∩C(X⊤)) degrees of freedom. It is identically zero iff no nonzero linear combination of the constrained functions is estimable.

prp-ss-no-intercept.html: For any model matrix X, with Y^=My and ε^=(I−M)y, ∑i(yi−y¯)2=∑i(y^i−y¯)2+∑iε^i2−2y¯∑iε^i. The last term vanishes for every y iff 1∈C(X).

prp-ss-tested-regression.title: Hypotheses of sequential and partial sums of squares
prp-ss-tested-regression.title_html: Hypotheses of sequential and partial sums of squares
prp-ss-tested-regression.html:
Let X=[X0,…,Xk] have full column rank and μ=∑lXlβl.

  1. The partial sum of squares of Xj addresses βj=0: (M−M(−j))μ=0 iff βj=0.

  2. The sequential sum of squares of Xj addresses βj+(X~j⊤X~j)−1X~j⊤∑l>jXlβl=0,X~j=(I−Mj−1)Xj. This is βj=0 whenever the later terms have zero coefficients, or whenever X~j⊤Xl=0 for all l>j.

thm-ss-adding.title: Adding regressors
thm-ss-adding.html:
Let W=[X,Z] have full column rank p+t, let C=(X⊤X)−1, β^=CX⊤y, and R=I−XCX⊤. Then:

  1. Z⊤RZ is positive definite;

  2. the least squares coefficients of the enlarged model are γ^=(Z⊤RZ)−1Z⊤Ry,β^W=β^−Lγ^,L=CX⊤Z;

  3. the residual sum of squares falls by SS(Z∣X)=y⊤RZ(Z⊤RZ)−1Z⊤Ry=γ^⊤Z⊤Ry=γ^⊤(Z⊤RZ)γ^;

  4. if Cov(Y)=σ2I, then Cov(γ^)=σ2(Z⊤RZ)−1, Cov(β^W,γ^)=−LCov(γ^) and Cov(β^W)=σ2[C+L(Z⊤RZ)−1L⊤].

thm-ss-decomposition.title: The analysis of variance identity
thm-ss-decomposition.html:
Let V1,…,Vk be an analysis of variance decomposition of C(X), with projections P1,…,Pk and dimensions r1,…,rk. Then:

  1. PiPj=0 for i≠j, P1+⋯+Pk=M, and I=P1+P2+⋯+Pk+(I−M), a sum of k+1 mutually orthogonal projections;

  2. for every y∈Rn the vectors P1y,…,Pky,(I−M)y are mutually orthogonal and ‖y‖2=‖P1y‖2+⋯+‖Pky‖2+‖(I−M)y‖2;{#eq-ss-anova-identity}

  3. ri=rank(Pi)=tr(Pi), r1+⋯+rk=r, and the error space has dimension tr(I−M)=n−r;

  4. if the columns of Qi (n×ri) form an orthonormal basis of Vi, then ‖Piy‖2=‖Qi⊤y‖2 is a sum of ri squares, and together with an orthonormal basis Qk+1 of the error space the matrix U=[Q1,…,Qk+1] is orthogonal;

  5. the subspaces Wj=V1⊕⋯⊕Vj form a chain W1⊆⋯⊆Wk=C(X) with projections Nj=P1+⋯+Pj, and Pj=Nj−Nj−1 (with N0=0). Conversely, every chain {0}=W0⊆W1⊆⋯⊆Wk=C(X) gives an analysis of variance decomposition with Vj=Wj−1⊥∩Wj.

thm-ss-expected-mean-squares.title: Expected mean squares
thm-ss-expected-mean-squares.html:
Let V1,…,Vk be an analysis of variance decomposition of C(X), with projections Pi and dimensions ri, and let E(Y)=μ, Cov(Y)=σ2I.

  1. E(Y⊤PiY)=σ2ri+‖Piμ‖2, so the mean square of Vi has expectation E(MSi)=σ2+‖Piμ‖2ri.{#eq-ss-ems}

  2. E(SSE)=σ2(n−r)+‖(I−M)μ‖2, so E(s2)=σ2 iff μ∈C(X).

  3. If μ=Xβ with X=[X0,…,Xk] partitioned into terms, the partial sum of squares of Xj has ESS(Xj∣X(−j))=σ2dj+βj⊤Xj⊤(I−M(−j))Xjβj, with dj=rank(M−M(−j)), and the sequential sum of squares of Xj has ESS(Xj∣X0,…,Xj−1)=σ2dj′+‖(Mj−Mj−1)Xβ‖2, with dj′=rank(Mj−Mj−1).

  4. If moreover Y is normal, then Var(Y⊤PiY)=2σ4ri+4σ2‖Piμ‖2, and the sums of squares of different subspaces, including the error space, are uncorrelated.

thm-ss-hypothesis.title: Sum of squares of a linear hypothesis
thm-ss-hypothesis.title_html: Sum of squares of a linear hypothesis
thm-ss-hypothesis.html:
Let Λ be a p×q matrix of rank q such that each entry of Λ⊤β is estimable, so that Λ=X⊤T for some n×q matrix T=[ρ1,…,ρq] (@def-est-estimable, @thm-proj-invariant-functions). Let G be any generalized inverse of X⊤X, let β^ be any least squares estimate, and let d∈Rq. Then:

  1. Λ⊤β^ and Λ⊤GΛ do not depend on the choices of β^ and G, and Λ⊤GΛ is positive definite;

  2. the subspace S0={Xb:Λ⊤b=0} of C(X) has orthogonal complement in C(X) equal to C(MT), of dimension q, and the projection onto C(MT) is MT(Λ⊤GΛ)−1T⊤M;

  3. the minimum of ‖y−Xb‖2 over {b:Λ⊤b=d} exceeds SSE by SSH=(Λ⊤β^−d)⊤(Λ⊤GΛ)−1(Λ⊤β^−d).{#eq-ss-hypothesis}

thm-ss-orthogonal-design.title: Orthogonal designs
thm-ss-orthogonal-design.html:
For a model X=[1,X1,…,Xk], the following are equivalent:

  1. the centred subspaces V1,…,Vk are mutually orthogonal;

  2. M=P0+PV1+⋯+PVk;

  3. for every j and every y, the marginal and partial sums of squares agree: SS(Xj∣1)=SS(Xj∣X(−j));

  4. for every y, the marginal sums of squares add up to the regression sum of squares: ∑jSS(Xj∣1)=SS(X1,…,Xk∣1).

When they hold, SS(Xj∣1,XS)=‖PVjy‖2 for every set S of other terms. In particular the sequential sum of squares of Xj is the same in every order, and it equals the partial and the Type II sums of squares of Xj.

thm-ss-partial-r2.title: Partial R^2, F and t
thm-ss-partial-r2.title_html: Partial R2, F and t
thm-ss-partial-r2.html:
With the notation of @def-ss-partial-r2, let r1=rank(X1), r=rank(X), q=r−r1>0, s2=SSE(X)/(n−r), and let F=[SS(X∣X1)/q]/s2. Then:

  1. 1−R2=(1−R12)(1−RX∣X12), where R2 and R12 belong to the two models;

  2. RX∣X12=qFqF+n−r;

  3. if X=[X1,xj] adds one column, then RX∣X12=tj2tj2+n−r, and it equals the squared sample correlation between the residuals (I−M1)y and (I−M1)xj;

  4. for a chain C(1)=C(X0)⊆C(X1)⊆⋯⊆C(Xk), 1−Rk2=∏j=1k(1−RXj∣Xj−12).

thm-ss-proportional.title: Proportional frequencies
thm-ss-proportional.html: In a two-way layout with factor A at a levels, factor B at b levels, cell counts nij, and all row totals ni⋅ and column totals n⋅j positive, the centred subspaces of A and B are orthogonal iff nij=ni⋅n⋅jnfor all i,j.{#eq-ss-proportional}

thm-ss-r2-max-correlation.title: R is the largest correlation with a linear combination
thm-ss-r2-max-correlation.title_html: R is the largest correlation with a linear combination
thm-ss-r2-max-correlation.html: Suppose 1∈C(X) and y is not constant. For every b such that Xb is not constant, corr(y,Xb)2≤R2. If R2>0, equality holds iff Xb=aY^+c1 for some a≠0 and some c, and the correlation corr(y,Xb) is maximized, with value R, by the fitted values themselves. If R2=0, every such correlation is zero.

thm-ss-r2-null.title: The distribution of R^2
thm-ss-r2-null.title_html: The distribution of R2
thm-ss-r2-null.html:
Let Y∼Nn(μ,σ2I) with μ∈C(X), 1∈C(X) and 1<r=rank(X)<n. Let F=[SSR/(r−1)]/[SSE/(n−r)] and γ=‖(M−P1)μ‖2/σ2. Then:

  1. R2=(r−1)F(r−1)F+n−r, and F∼F(r−1,n−r,γ);

  2. if μ∈span(1), so that no regressor matters, then R2∼Beta(r−12,n−r2) and E(R2)=r−1n−1.

thm-ss-restricted.title: Restricted least squares
thm-ss-restricted.html: Let X have full column rank, C=(X⊤X)−1, and let Λ (p×q) have rank q. For any d∈Rq, the unique minimizer of ‖y−Xb‖2 subject to Λ⊤b=d is β^H=β^−CΛ(Λ⊤CΛ)−1(Λ⊤β^−d), and ‖y−Xβ^H‖2=SSE+‖X(β^−β^H)‖2, where the last term equals SSH of @eq-ss-hypothesis with G=C.

thm-ss-single-df.title: Orthogonal single-degree-of-freedom sums of squares
thm-ss-single-df.html:
Let λ1,…,λs be nonzero vectors with λk⊤β estimable, so that λk=X⊤ρk, and let G be a generalized inverse of X⊤X.

  1. The sum of squares for λk⊤β=0 is SSk=(λk⊤β^)2λk⊤Gλk=‖Pvky‖2,vk=Mρk, the squared length of the projection of y onto the line spanned by vk.

  2. vh⊤vk=λh⊤Gλk. If λh⊤Gλk=0 for all h≠k, the lines are mutually orthogonal, and ∑kSSk is the sum of squares for the joint hypothesis λ1⊤β=⋯=λs⊤β=0, on s degrees of freedom.

  3. Conversely, every orthonormal basis u1,…,us of a subspace of C(X) arises in this way, with λk=X⊤uk.

thm-ss-two-way-hypotheses.title: What the sums of squares for a main effect test
thm-ss-two-way-hypotheses.title_html: What the sums of squares for a main effect test
thm-ss-two-way-hypotheses.html:
In the two-way layout with all nij≥1:

  1. the sequential sum of squares SS(A∣μ) of A entered first addresses μ¯1w=⋯=μ¯aw;

  2. the Type III sum of squares of A addresses μ¯1⋅=⋯=μ¯a⋅;

  3. the partial sum of squares of the columns of A under reference-level coding (indicators of levels 2,…,a of A and 2,…,b of B, and their products for AB) addresses μ11=μ21=⋯=μa1, the equality of the A means at the first level of B;

  4. the Type II sum of squares SS(A∣μ,B) addresses a hypothesis that, when the cell means are additive (μij=αi+βj), is equivalent to α1=⋯=αa.

Each sum of squares equals the sum of squares @eq-ss-hypothesis of the hypothesis it addresses, in the cell-means model.
